facts.claim: Noah Kahan and Gabe Simon wrote and produced "Northern Attitude" together.
It was released on September 16, 2022, as the second single from Kahan's third studio album, Stick Season.
Credits list Gabe Simon on guitar, bass, drums, mandolin, organ, percussion, piano and background vocals. Kahan is credited on vocals, guitar and background vocals, and Konrad Snyder on piano.
Ryan Hewitt mixed the track, Ted Jensen mastered it, and Jordon Silva assisted on the mix. Mercury Records/Republic Records released it.
Kahan has called Vermont "one of the loneliest places to live in the world." He said he wanted to write a song about that loneliness and how it shapes the way we approach relationships.
The song opens the Stick Season album. It describes small-town life in rural Vermont, a yearning to escape, and the pull to stay where you were raised.
Kahan began writing the Stick Season record in his hometown of Strafford, Vermont, in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. He described the album as a "love letter to New England."

A duet version with Irish singer-songwriter Hozier was released on November 10, 2023, and appears on the Stick Season (Forever) edition. Hozier takes the second verse and keeps Kahan's original lyrics.
Kahan and Hozier met when both played the Iron Blossom Festival in Richmond, Virginia, in late August 2023. They first performed the song together at a Nashville show in October 2023.
Noah Kahan was born January 1, 1997, in Strafford, Vermont. Stick Season (2022), his third album, was his mainstream commercial breakthrough after I Was / I Am (2021) and his 2019 debut Busyhead.

research.lineage: The song sits in the contemporary folk-pop and indie-folk wave that Kahan's Stick Season helped popularize, with lyrics rooted in rural New England and Vermont small-town life.

draft:
**Northern Attitude** opens on small talk. Noah Kahan runs through the questions you ask someone you haven't seen in years: how have you been, have you settled down, are you proud, where are the kids now. Then the verse stops asking and starts summing up. You build a boat, you build a life, and the losses follow in the same flat rhythm, as if they were just the next items on the list. In the second verse "friends" turns into "kids," and by then the portrait has slid into something darker: a person gone lost and getting high, alone and "Scared to live, scared to die." It's never clear whether Kahan is describing an old neighbor, a parent, or the life he can see waiting for himself. The song works because it never settles that question.

The chorus is where the feeling breaks open, and it's half apology, half alibi: "Forgive my northern attitude / Oh, I was raised out in the cold." Kahan is asking for patience and making an excuse in the same breath. The coldness is admitted, then blamed on the weather, on a place where the sun doesn't come up until summer. Kahan has called Vermont "one of the loneliest places to live in the world," and said he wanted to write about how that loneliness shapes the way people handle relationships. You can hear it in the chorus's opening worry about getting too close and not being what someone hoped for. That isn't standoffishness. It's fear of being found wanting. In the last chorus the pronoun flips to "If you get too close," and the defense now faces outward, as if the walls have finally gone all the way up.

The sound pushes against all that withdrawal. Acoustic guitar strums under a bright electric melody line, bass and drums drive at a medium-fast clip, and the mix is full and polished, with an open room around it. Kahan's voice is slightly raspy and direct, with no harmonies to soften it, so the confession lands without cushioning. A shouted count-off ("three, four") kicks the second chorus in like a band at a basement show, and the wordless "oh-oh-ah-ah" stretch gives everyone in the room something to shout who can't quite say the rest.

Kahan and Gabe Simon wrote and produced the song together, with Simon covering much of the playing. It opens *Stick Season*, the record Kahan began in his hometown of Strafford, Vermont, in 2020 and called a "love letter to New England." The record became his breakthrough and helped push a wave of folk-pop rooted in small places. Hozier later took the second verse on a duet version and kept every word.

It sticks because it hands you a stadium-sized chorus to sing along to, and the thing you're singing is an apology for not knowing how to let anyone in.
